name: LifeWire TrueRead Emotional Context Implant
body_location: cranial temporal lobe — bilateral micro-array with subdermal facial nerve sensor cluster
description:
The TrueRead is a bilateral micro-array implanted in the temporal lobes alongside a distributed mesh of subdermal pressure and myoelectric sensors embedded across the upper cheeks, brow, and jaw line. Together, these components read the user's social environment in real time: facial micro-expressions, postural tension, vocal cadence shifts, and autonomic cues such as pupil dilation and skin flush are processed through LifeWire's proprietary SocialFrame inference engine, which runs locally on the implant's onboard co-processor. The resulting interpretation — rendered as a soft ambient overlay in peripheral awareness rather than a visual HUD — manifests as a kind of trained intuition, a gentle knowing that the person across from you is nervous, or bored, or holding something back. The system does not read minds; it reads bodies, and it does so with approximately 78% accuracy on baseline emotional states, improving with use as the implant calibrates to the user's social context and cultural environment over several months of passive learning.

The TrueRead's primary market is broad and largely quiet about it — neurodivergent individuals who process social cues atypically make up roughly 40% of the install base, many citing it as life-changing in the same register as corrective lenses or hearing aids. But it's also deeply popular among customer-facing workers — hospitality staff, social workers, teachers, caregivers, negotiators — anyone whose livelihood depends on reading a room. In daily life, the experience is subtle: you don't see a readout, you just suddenly find yourself a little better at noticing when a friend is struggling even as they say they're fine, or when a client's polite tone masks real frustration. Most users describe a gradual shift over weeks — the world feels slightly more legible, social exhaustion diminishes, and interactions feel less like guesswork. For those who grew up feeling perpetually out of step with unspoken social rules, the TrueRead is often described not as an enhancement, but as something that was always missing.
installation_requirements: Outpatient clinic; approximately 90-minute procedure under local anesthesia for sensor mesh placement and temporal array insertion; no overnight stay required
maintenance: Firmware update every 6 months via clinic tap or certified LifeWire kiosk; annual calibration check recommended; sensor mesh is self-maintaining and does not require replacement under normal use

side_effects: Mild emotional bleed during calibration period — users occasionally feel ambient distress or excitement that is not their own, typically resolving after 6-8 weeks
Heightened social fatigue in crowded environments during the first month as the system learns filtering thresholds
Occasional false-positive reads on familiar faces, leading to unwarranted concern for people who are fine
Some users report difficulty 'switching off' the ambient awareness in contexts where they'd prefer not to know — a skill that requires deliberate practice
cultural_context: The TrueRead occupies an interesting social position in GLMZ: it is common enough that most people know someone who has one, but uncommon enough that it is not yet assumed. Among neurodivergent communities across all tiers it carries almost no stigma whatsoever — it is spoken of in the same breath as stimulant prescriptions or therapy, a practical tool for navigating a world not built for every kind of mind. In Tier 1 and 2 communities it is frequently the first significant cyberware purchase a person makes, often financed through VitaCore's community health subsidy programs or purchased refurbished. In corporate Tier 3 and 4 environments, there is a quiet undercurrent of unease around TrueRead users — not overt prejudice, but a low-level awareness that this person may notice things you'd rather keep private, which occasionally translates into subtle professional friction. Among the young, the implant carries no particular fashion valence — it's invisible and unannounced, which is either its greatest virtue or its only flaw depending on who you ask. The street name 'the undercurrent' reflects how most users describe its effect: not a spotlight on other people's feelings, but a steady, quiet current running beneath every conversation.
known_users: Neurodivergent individuals across all tiers — autism spectrum, ADHD, social anxiety disorders
Hospitality and service workers in Tier 2-3 environments
Social workers, counselors, and community health advocates
Mid-level corporate negotiators and account managers in Tier 3
Parents of young children who want to better read non-verbal distress signals
Performers and public speakers who need to gauge live audience response
story_hooks: A player character with a TrueRead begins picking up consistent low-level fear signals from a coworker who insists everything is fine — the implant's calibration suggests the signals are genuine and sustained, raising the question of whether the coworker is being coerced or watched

A Tier 1 community organizer with a TrueRead notices that a city official attending a public meeting is projecting all the microexpression markers of guilt and concealment — not nervousness, which would be expected, but something heavier — and has to decide what to do with an impression that isn't evidence

A firmware update pushed by LifeWire introduces a subtle new feature that users didn't consent to: aggregated anonymized emotional environment data fed back to a corporate client for 'venue atmosphere analytics' — and one user's implant starts flagging the data collection as anomalous
